items.title: L’autre visage du miracle chinois est dans le Hunan
items.description: Connaissez-vous trois provinces chinoises ? Pour comprendre la Chine de Xi, il faut sortir de Pékin et de Shanghai. Notre nouvelle série part à la rencontre des espaces où se construit une autre figure du futur. Pour recevoir cette série qui nous a déjà amené du Sichuan au Zhejiang en passant par le Guangxi , abonnez-vous au Grand Continent . Dans votre boîte mail à partir de 8 euros par mois À Zhuzhou, ville industrielle typique de la province du Hunan, dans le centre de la Chine, un viaduc ferroviaire traverse le cœur de la ville. On dit souvent qu’elle a été « amenée ici par les trains ». Employée dans toute la région, cette formule est peu à peu devenue un motif de fierté locale. Des « 156 projets » à la réforme du marché Il fut un temps où l’entreprise ferroviaire s’occupait de tout. Les administrations et les usines ne se contentaient pas de fournir des emplois, mais géraient aussi des écoles, des dispensaires et des complexes résidentiels pour les familles de leurs employés. Tout a radicalement changé peu après 1993, avec le passage à l’économie de marché. Les écoles primaires autrefois réservées aux enfants des cheminots sont désormais ouvertes à tous. Dans la banlieue sud, sur le site désigné par le code « 331 », un collège a remplacé l’usine d’armement édifiée sous le régime nationaliste. Pendant la Guerre froide, l’usine 331 (aujourd’hui China Aero-Engine Corporation Southern Industrial Co., Ltd.) faisait partie des « 156 projets » industriels et miniers clefs importés d’Union soviétique et d’Europe de l’Est au cours du premier plan quinquennal (1953-1957). Ils couvraient, entre autres, les secteurs du charbon, de l’électricité, des machines et des métaux non ferreux. En 1960, lorsque l’Union soviétique a retiré son aide, 133 d’entre eux avaient été achevés et mis en service 156 Key Projects »(150 projets ont effectivement été menés à bien).'> 1 “156项”建设项目对中国工业化的历史贡献 », Honghuiwang , 27 mai 2022. (921 projets de construction dépassant le seuil fixé ont été réalisés au cours du premier plan quinquennal).'> 2 . C’était l’un des plus vastes dispositifs d’aide extérieure du bloc socialiste. L’Union soviétique avait envoyé 14 experts à Zhuzhou, ainsi que des plans et des machines. Elle y a aussi laissé des bâtiments en briques rouges au style reconnaissable. Le 16 août 1954, c’est à l’usine 331 qu’a été construit le premier moteur d’avion chinois. Deux mois plus tard, Mao Zedong a personnellement signé une lettre de félicitations 三台发动机，带你了解70年航空发动机进化史 », New Hunan , 30 octobre 2024.'> 3 党史上的湖南之最丨​株洲三三一厂试制成功中国第一台航空发动机 », New Hunan , 8 avril 2021.'> 4 et son texte, gravé dans la pierre, rappelle encore aujourd’hui cet épisode. Suivant ce modèle, Zhuzhou a aussi construit l’usine 601 (une usine de carbure cémenté), une centrale électrique et une usine de lavage du charbon. Le programme d’aide fournissait des technologies, un financement et des conseils d’experts. Il a aussi permis à de nombreux techniciens chinois de se former en Union soviétique. Mais les relations sino-soviétiques se sont dégradées. En juillet 1960, l’aide a pris fin brusquement. Moscou a rappelé l’ensemble des 1 390 experts en poste en Chine, repartis avec leurs documents techniques 湖湘广记｜见证中苏友好的专家楼 », Tencent News , 23 mai 2022 (l'usine 601 est l'usine de carbure cémentée de Zhuzhou).'> 5 苏联援华156项工程的前因后果 », chronique sur Zhihu , 17 janvier 2019 (1 390 experts soviétiques ont été rappelés de Chine).'> 6 . En 1964, alors que la guerre menée par les États-Unis au Vietnam s'intensifiait, Mao Zedong, inquiet pour la sécurité nationale, a lancé la « construction du Troisième Front ». Le plan consistait à mobiliser les ressources de toute la nation pour déplacer vers l’intérieur du pays, des sites industriels et militaires clefs implantés sur la côte. Ces régions étaient mal desservies, mais les usines pouvaient s’y abriter dans les montagnes et les grottes. Le Hunan faisait partie de ce plan. Cette campagne nationale visant à doter le pays d’une base industrielle autonome a atteint son apogée entre 1965 et 1966. Selon les statistiques officielles, l’ouest du Hunan a construit 71 projets de grande et moyenne envergure au cours de cette période, avec des investissements s’élevant à 4,5 milliards de yuans, soit plus de 70 % des dépenses d’équipement de la province à l’époque. Ces projets n’étaient pas rentables sur le plan économique. Ils ont néanmoins posé les bases de l’essor ultérieur du Hunan en tant que grande province industrielle 三线建设掀起热潮：改变湖南国防地位和工业布局 », Département provincial de l'industrie et des technologies de l'information du Hunan, 15 avril 2021.'> 7 . Mais avec le déclenchement de la Révolution culturelle en 1966, le chantier du Troisième Front a subi revers et perturbations à répétition. De nombreux projets ont été totalement ou partiellement interrompus. Le Troisième Front a vu grandir une génération d’« enfants des complexes industriels », élevés au milieu d’une pollution intense. Il a surtout produit des familles étroitement dépendantes du système d’État. Lorsque les entreprises publiques ont été restructurées et que le pays s’est tourné vers les réformes de marché à la fin des années 1990, ces familles ont été laissées pour compte. Beaucoup d’ouvriers, réaffectés ou licenciés encore jeunes, sont partis tenter leur chance comme travailleurs migrants dans le sud, à Shenzhen ou à Guangzhou. Encore aujourd’hui, certains envient ceux partis vers le Sud, se disant : « Si seulement j’avais franchi le pas à l’époque, ma vie ne se serait pas dégradée à ce point. » Mais rares sont ceux qui, là-bas, ont vraiment fait fortune. Géographie et industrie du Hunan Les voies ferrées, les maisons en briques rouges, les proches au chômage… Pour raconter le Hunan, il faut replacer ces images dans leur contexte historique. Fin 2025, le Hunan comptait 64,92 millions de résidents permanents, à peu près autant que la France. En 2025, son PIB atteignait quelque 5 530 milliards de yuans (près de 700 milliards d’euros). Cela le classait au dixième rang en Chine et en faisait une puissance économique majeure de la région centrale. Mais la province est très peuplée : son PIB par habitant en 2025 était d’environ 84 600 yuans (environ 11 000 euros). Ce chiffre était inférieur à la moyenne nationale (autour de 12 900 euros) et représentait moins des deux tiers de celui des provinces côtières comme le Jiangsu et le Zhejiang 湖南省2025年国民经济和社会发展统计公报 », gouvernement provincial du Hunan (population résidente permanente en fin d'année : 64,92 millions).'> 8 2025年湖南GDP突破5.5万亿元 同比增长4.8 % », Bureau provincial des statistiques du Hunan , 28 janvier 2026. (5 530,865 milliards de yuans).'> 9 31省份2025年GDP排名出炉：谁靠前？谁垫底 ? », Caijing , 2 février 2026 (le Hunan occupe la dixième place avec 5 530,9 milliards de yuans).'> 10 2025年湖南省各市州GDP数据公布，常德市GDP名义增速最高 », NetEase , 26 février 2026.(PIB par habitant du Hunan : 84 583 yuans ; moyenne nationale : 99 665 yuans).'> 11 . Le Hunan se situe au sud du cours moyen du Yangtsé. Il abrite le lac Dongting, le deuxième plus grand lac d’eau douce de Chine. Autour du lac, le relief est plat et sillonné de rivières. Son climat de mousson subtropicale apporte à la fois pluie et chaleur. Ces conditions en font un terrain idéal pour la culture du riz et l’élevage de poissons d’eau douce. C’est pourquoi le bassin du lac Dongting est surnommé la « Terre du poisson et du riz » de Chine. Les profondes racines agricoles du Hunan confèrent à la société une base stable. Aujourd’hui, l’agriculture ne représente plus qu’environ 9 % de l’économie, alors que l’industrie pèse quelque 29 % du PIB provincial et assure environ 41 % de sa croissance. L’industrie fournit en outre 42,7 % des recettes fiscales 湖南省2024年国民经济和社会发展统计公报 », Bureau provincial des statistiques du Hunan, 24 mars 2025 (structure en trois secteurs : 9,2 : 36,7 : 54,1 ; la valeur ajoutée industrielle représentait 29,3 % du PIB et contribuait à hauteur de 41,5 % à la croissance économique).'> 12 5大类21项发展指标！湖南明确“十五五”制造业发展蓝图 », Changsha Evening News Online , 3 juin 2026 (en 2025, la valeur ajoutée du secteur manufacturier représentait 26,4 % du PIB et les impôts industriels 42,7 % des recettes fiscales totales).'> 13 . La géographie du Hunan a aussi façonné une culture culinaire distinctive. L’une de ses principales caractéristiques est le goût pour les épices, le piment notamment. On dit qu’il chasse l’humidité du corps, un atout précieux sous un climat aussi lourd et moite. À une époque où il était difficile de conserver les aliments, les Hunanais ont mis au point des techniques de fumage, de salaison et de marinade. Cet amour des épices s’est même inscrit dans le caractère politique de la province. Mao Zedong a un jour fait une boutade largement citée : « Pas de piment, pas de révolution. » Ce n’était qu’à moitié une plaisanterie. Le pragmatisme, l’audace et la ténacité (« baman ») sont bel et bien devenus des traits de l’identité des Hunanais. L’histoire moderne de la province a vu naître de grandes figures politiques et militaires : les chefs de l’Armée du Hunan à la fin de la dynastie Qing, Zeng Guofan et Zuo Zongtang, les figures de la Révolution de 1911, Huang Xing et Song Jiaoren, ainsi que plusieurs maréchaux originaires du Hunan comptant parmi les généraux fondateurs de la République populaire. Dans son ouvrage Provincial Patriots : The Hunanese and Modern China , Stephen R. Platt affirme qu’il ne s’agit pas d’un hasard. Selon lui, les Hunanais ont redécouvert, dans la pensée de Wang Fuzhi, une philosophie pragmatique et ouverte sur le monde, ainsi qu’une conscience nationale. La victoire de l’Armée du Hunan sur la Révolte des Taiping a également permis de tisser un vaste réseau de liens régionaux qui a fourni les talents nécessaires à l’organisation de la Révolution de 1911 Provincial Patriots : The Hunanese and Modern China (édition chinoise publiée par Social Sciences Academic Press, collection Oracle) ; voir également l'interview « Stephen Platt : Les Hunanais ont marqué l'histoire chinoise à des moments décisifs », The Paper , 18 novembre 2025.'> 14 . Après le départ des Soviétiques, le Hunan s’est appuyé sur la base industrielle héritée du Troisième Front. Il a progressivement fait des engins de chantier une chaîne industrielle clef à développer. À partir de 2000, la Chine a construit des routes, des ponts et des bâtiments à une échelle sans précédent. Portée par cette vague, la demande en pelles mécaniques et en grues a explosé. Les groupes de Changsha, Sany et Zoomlion, sont ainsi devenus des fournisseurs de premier plan d’équipements industriels de base. Les médias locaux aiment utiliser le terme « Armée du Hunan » en référence à l’armée de Zeng Guofan, pour désigner les fleurons industriels de la province, leurs engins de chantier symbolisant des troupes. En 2017, Changsha a été la première ville à mettre en place le « système du chef de chaîne » (链长制). Dans ce modèle de gouvernance, un responsable gouvernemental fait office de « chef de chaîne » et aide à coordonner les terrains, les capitaux et les politiques. Une entreprise chef de file endosse le rôle de « maître de la chaîne », et se charge de l’innovation et de l’expansion commerciale. Le dispositif a en partie amélioré le taux d’approvisionnement local, mais il a aussi entraîné des dérives, comme un interventionnisme administratif excessif. En septembre 2020, Xi Jinping s’est rendu dans le Hunan et a défini la stratégie des « Trois Hauts plateaux et des Quatre nouvelles missions ». Construire un « haut plateau de fabrication de pointe d’importance nationale » est ainsi devenu une priorité pour la province Le système du chef de chaîne : mise en pratique et problèmes », Institut d'économie industrielle, Académie chinoise des sciences sociales, 28 avril 2024 (C'est à Changsha que le concept de « chef de chaîne » a été proposé pour la première fois, le 23 novembre 2017).'> 15 湖湘潮 百年颂 | 习近平总书记到湖南考察:赋予湖南“三个高地”战略定位和“四新”使命任务 », gouvernement provincial du Hunan, 19 juillet 2021 (inspection effectuée du 16 au 18 septembre 2020).'> 16 . Derrière la capitale du divertissement, des inégalités qui se creusent Le Hunan est aussi surnommé la « capitale du divertissement », dont Changsha, son chef-lieu, est la vitrine. C’est sur la chaîne de télévision par satellite du Hunan (le Hunan Broadcasting System) qu’a commencé l’émergence de Changsha en tant que haut lieu de la culture virale. Au début des années 1990, cette chaîne n’était encore qu’une chaîne provinciale. Elle vivait des publicités pour l’agriculture et l'élevage. Son chiffre d’affaires annuel était inférieur à 60 millions de yuans (environ 7 à 8 millions d’euros). Les habitants la surnommaient avec humour la « chaîne des engrais et des aliments pour animaux ». Mais en 1993, Wei Wenbin, le nouveau directeur de la chaîne, a engagé des réformes. Selon lui, c’était le divertissement qui faisait alors le plus défaut en Chine 湖南广电原局长魏文彬去世，曾推出现象级节目《快乐大本营》《超级女声》 », Tencent News , 29 janvier 2026 (nommé secrétaire du Parti et directeur du Bureau de la radio et de la télévision du Hunan en 1993 ; le chiffre d'affaires annuel de la chaîne était inférieur à 60 millions de yuans).'> 17 . 1993, c’est aussi la veille de la restructuration des entreprises d’État. La vague de réformes qui allait fermer les usines des villes industrielles a, dans le même temps, ouvert les vannes des recettes publicitaires de la chaîne. La chaîne s’est alors engouffrée dans le divertissement. Happy Camp, une émission de variétés diffusée le week-end, a été lancée en juillet 1997. Elle a accompagné l’enfance de plusieurs générations de Chinois et a forgé une mémoire collective. En 1998, le feuilleton historique My Fair Princess , produit par Hunan Economics Channel, réunissait une part d’audience moyenne de 45 %, avec des pics à plus de 58 %, un record pour une série de la chaîne. Un quart de siècle plus tard, la série, adaptée d’un roman de la Taïwanaise Qiong Yao, est encore rediffusée chaque été et reste en tête des audiences 风暴眼丨那个创办《快乐大本营》的人，离开了 », Ifeng Finance, 29 janvier 2026 (La série « My Fair Princess » a enregistré une part d'audience moyenne de 45 % sur la chaîne Hunan Economics Channel, avec un pic supérieur à 58 %).'> 18 . En 2004, Hunan TV a créé une émission intitulée Super Girl , un concours de talents destiné au grand public, dont le format s’apparentait à celui de « Star Academy ». La deuxième saison, en 2005, a connu un succès sans précédent, avec plus de 150 000 personnes inscrites lors de cinq sélections régionales. Pour la première fois, des centaines de millions de téléspectateurs ont goûté au frisson de désigner eux-mêmes la gagnante 那个创办《快乐大本营》的人，留下了中国电视行业的“电视湘军” », Sohu : 3 février 2026 (en 2005, la deuxième saison comptait cinq épreuves régionales et plus de 150 000 inscriptions).'> 19 . C’est sur ce terreau télévisuel que Changsha est devenue une fabrique de tendances. De nombreuses personnes formées au sein du système audiovisuel et médiatique du Hunan ont par la suite contribué à la création des nouvelles marques grand public de la province. Ces dernières accordent de l’importance aux médias et à la création culturelle, comprennent les jeunes et savent comment créer le buzz. Prenons l’exemple de la marque locale de thé Cha Yan Yue Se, qui a gagné en popularité il y a quelques années. Au début, elle a concentré ses points de vente à Changsha et s’est fait connaître sur des plateformes telles que Douyin (le TikTok chinois), suscitant un engouement porté par le « marketing de la rareté ». Depuis 2022, la marque s’est progressivement étendue à des villes comme Wuhan, Nankin, Chongqing et Shenzhen. Son nom poétique et ses boutiques au style traditionnel semblent avoir répondu au désir d’identité culturelle des jeunes. En se promenant aujourd’hui dans Changsha, on voit souvent de longues files d’attente devant de nombreuses marques et boutiques. Outre le thé aux perles, les spécialités nocturnes du Hunan comptent le « tofu puant » (臭豆腐) frit et poivré, et le kouwei xia (口味虾) , écrevisses noyées dans du piment. Cette frénésie de consommation tient notamment au coût de la vie, relativement modéré. En 2016, alors que les prix de l’immobilier grimpaient en flèche à l’échelle nationale, Changsha a mis en place des restrictions sur la revente et des réglementations sur le prix des terrains afin d’empêcher la spéculation immobilière. Selon l’étude 2020 de l’Institut de recherche E-House sur le ratio prix de l’immobilier/revenu dans 50 villes chinoises, celui de Changsha n’était que de 6,2. Ce chiffre la classait dernière parmi les 50 villes : en d’autres termes, une famille pouvait acheter un appartement avec un peu plus de six ans de revenus. La même année, le ratio de Shenzhen atteignait 35,2 网红城市长沙的低房价是如何炼成的？ | 楼市地理 » Yicai (Institut de recherche E-House, Rapport 2020 sur le rapport prix de l'immobilier/revenu dans 50 villes chinoises : Changsha 6,2, Shenzhen 35,2).'> 20 . Cette croissance est très inégale dans la province. Ainsi, en 2023, le PIB par habitant de Changsha représentait 1,82 fois la moyenne provinciale. Ce multiple la plaçait en tête de toutes les capitales provinciales chinoises, même s'il était en baisse par rapport à l’année précédente (1,86). En 2025, Changsha continuait de représenter 28,5 % du PIB provincial et cet énorme déséquilibre interne pourrait encore s’accentuer dans les années à venir 2025年湖南各市州GDP排名：长沙一城独大，张家界垫底，邵阳名义增速为负 », Tencent News , 4 mars 2026 (Changsha représentait 28,5 % du PIB provincial).'> 21 . Se tourner vers l’étranger : un levier de croissance Le secteur immobilier chinois a connu un déclin brutal à la suite de la pandémie, et les investissements dans les infrastructures stagnent. Le secteur des machines industrielles du Hunan doit se réinventer et c’est désormais à l'international que se joue sa croissance. Depuis 2019, le Salon économique et commercial Chine-Afrique s’est installé à Changsha, où il s’est tenu à quatre reprises 第四届中国－非洲经贸博览会在湖南长沙开幕 », Xinhua / Baidu Baike , 13 juin 2025. Ce salon se tient à Changsha, dans la province du Hunan, depuis 2019 (la première édition a eu lieu du 27 au 29 juin 2019) ; la quatrième édition s'est déroulée à Changsha du 12 au 15 juin 2025.'> 22 . En 2020, la Zone pilote de libre-échange du Hunan a ouvert ses portes, avec pour objectif prioritaire la coopération avec l’Afrique Plan global pour la zone pilote de libre-échange de Chine (Hunan) », Conseil d’État / Bureau de la zone de libre-échange du Hunan , 23 octobre 2026.La zone a été officiellement créée en septembre 2020 et compte parmi ses principaux objectifs stratégiques l’exploration de nouvelles voies et de nouveaux mécanismes pour la coopération économique et commerciale sino-africaine (zone pionnière de coopération économique et commerciale approfondie entre la Chine et l’Afrique).'> 23 . En 2025, par exemple, le chiffre d’affaires à l’international de Sany Heavy Industry – l’un des plus grands fabricants chinois d’engins de chantier – s’est élevé à 55,86 milliards de yuans (environ 7 milliards d’euros), soit 64 % du total. Le chiffre d’affaires réalisé en Afrique a atteint 8,31 milliards de yuans (environ 1 milliard d’euros) 三一重工股份有限公司 2025 年年度报告 », CNINFO (code boursier 600031) : en 2025, le chiffre d'affaires de l'activité principale à l'international de la société s'élevait à 55,86 milliards de yuans, soit une hausse de 15,1 % par rapport à l'année précédente, représentant 64 % du chiffre d'affaires de l'activité principale dans le secteur des engins de chantier.'> 24 , en hausse de 55,29 % par rapport à l’année précédente. Les engins de chantier du Hunan sont aussi largement utilisés dans des projets d’infrastructure dans les pays participant à l’initiative « La Ceinture et la Route » (le programme mondial d’infrastructure et d’investissement de la Chine). De la ligne de tramway en Éthiopie aux mines de cuivre en Zambie, en passant par les autoroutes algériennes, on retrouve presque partout des machines sorties des usines du Hunan. Leur présence nourrit aussi, dans certains pays, des débats sur les conditions de travail et l’endettement. La ville que les trains avaient « amenée ici » voit donc aujourd’hui partir ses habitants et ses machines. Dans les années 1950, Zhuzhou recevait quatorze experts soviétiques ; elle exporte à présent ses engins de chantier, les rôles se sont inversés. Ce que ce passage laissera en Afrique, nul ne le sait encore. En 1960, personne ne savait non plus que les bâtiments de briques rouges des Soviétiques marqueraient encore la ville soixante ans plus tard. L’article L’autre visage du miracle chinois est dans le Hunan est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Les organisateurs veulent promouvoir la filière lait
items.description: A quelques jours du démarrage de la foire régionale de Sédhiou prévue du 06 au 14 novembre 2026 , les organisateurs ont affiché leur objectif. Ces derniers qui visent à accueillir 300 exposants ont mis l'accent sur la promotion de la filière lait. SEDHIOU – Le ton est donné. « Cette année nous visons un objectif de 300 exposants au moins », a lancé Ousseynou Diagne, secrétaire général de la chambre de commerce et d’industrie de Sédhiou, lors du lancement de la 3e édition de la foire commerciale, agricole et de service. L’événement va débuter du 6 au 14 novembre 2026 à Sédhiou. Faisant le point sur la préparation de ce rassemblement annuel, Aïda Mandiang, femme transformatrice, membre de la chambre de commerce de Sédhiou, estime que ce pari sera réussi jusqu’à obtenir même 400 voire 500 exposants. Pour elle, la région de Sédhiou regorge de nombreuses compétences qui mérite à l’occasion de ce rendez-vous révéler leur savoir-faire. « Avec toutes ces femmes et tous ces hommes qui sont là, dans la production et la valorisation des produits locaux, nous croyons fermement que nous allons atteindre ce but », a-t-elle persisté, lançant un appel à la mobilisation. Cette année, les organisateurs entendent mettre l’accent sur le lait local et ses produits dérivés. Ce choix, à en croire Ousseynou Diagne, a pour objectif de montrer au monde que la région regorge de produits laitiers assez satisfaisants pour alimenter le marché national. « Mais aussi de plaider pour l’assistance des éleveurs notamment ceux qui interviennent dans la volaille, le bovin entre autres », a-t-il soutenu. Région humide en raison de son important pluviomètre par an, Sédhiou a des atouts favorables au développement du fourrage essentiel pour l’alimentation du bétail. « Si nous sommes donc assistés dans le domaine de l'élevage, la région pourra avancer dans ce secteur », a insisté le secrétaire général de la chambre de commerce de Sédhiou. L’édition de cette année milite en faveur du raffermissement du bon voisinage. C’est dans ce sens que la Guinée Bissau prendra part à l’événement comme hôte d’honneur. « Nous avons la même culture, les mêmes langues, nous sommes le même peuple et cela va favoriser l’intégration régionale », a ajouté M. Diagne qui signale que des panels seront organisés tout au long de cet évènement. Jonas Souloubany BASSENE (correspondant)

items.title: Hina Javed murder case: In open letter to Punjab CM, victim's family again expresses mistrust in police probe
items.description: RAWALPINDI/ LAHORE: The victim’s family in the Hina Javed murder case has written an open letter to Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, again expressing their mistrust in the police investigation and calling for the formation of a judicial commission to probe the matter, it emerged on Sunday. Hina, a 45-year-old digital media executive, was found dead at her residence in Rawalpindi in August, with police noting signs of torture. Her husband and their domestic worker were arrested as Hina’s family accused them of murdering her while her father-in-law was questioned as part of the investigation. Earlier, her family had written to the National Commission on Human Rights, requesting intervention in the investigation of the murder case and alleging that the probe was compromised. On Saturday, when the Punjab CM was asked on X to look into the case, she responded: “I am keeping a close watch. The DNA test results and polygraph test suggest that the murder and rape were committed by the servant; however the investigation is ongoing.” In their letter, Hina’s family referred to Maryam’s post, claiming that the investigation “continues to shift blame away from” the victim’s husband. “We, the family of the late Hina Javed, write to you publicly because every effort to reach you directly has failed,” the letter began. It added: “The extent and brutality of torture […] tells you everything you need to know about this murder. It tells you about the rage and hate that went into it.” In its letter, the family said it had shared its concerns, reservations and objections regarding the police investigation committee probing the case and “we also tried repeatedly to meet or speak with you, but we were never able to reach you”. Referring to CM Maryam’s post on X, it claimed the DNA of Hina’s husband and father-in-law was found on her body. And the forensic reports of her husband’s laptop, as well as those of his and the domestic worker’s mobile phones, were pending; pertinent messages were deleted from Hina’s mobile; and the investigation “continues to shift blame away from” Hina’s husband and “points solely towards the domestic servant who is also guilty and party to the murder”, the family alleged. It also accused Hina’s husband of “planting evidence” in the case. According to the postmortem and DNA report analysis , evidence collected during the investigation indicated that Hina had been brutally tortured. The postmortem report noted blue marks on her hands and arms and a wound on her neck. Forensic evidence collected from the crime scene also matched the DNA samples of her husband and domestic servant, according to the DNA analysis report. The report said that the Y-STR profile — a DNA test that examines the Y chromosome — from Hina’s clothes found a mixture of DNA from at least three individuals, and her husband, father-in-law and domestic servant could not be excluded as contributors. The family requested CM Maryam to look into the case file in detail and see the evidence linking Hina’s husband “to the murder being ignored from day one”. The family also objected to the police investigation committee being “allowed to declare who is guilty and who is innocent before the case has gone to trial”. “That decision belongs to a court of law, not to the investigators. A body that both investigates and pronounces a verdict has a clear conflict of interest, and we have no confidence that justice will be served this way,” the family asserted. It rejected the findings of the police investigation committee and reiterated its demand for the immediate formation of a judicial commission for an “impartial investigation” of the murder case. “As a woman and as the chief executive of this province, we appeal to you to ensure that her killers are not shielded and that her family receives justice under the law,” the letter concluded. Responding to a post urging her to consider what Hina’s brother was saying, CM Maryam said, “Yes. Investigation has not concluded yet. We shall leave no stone unturned. I will also meet the family personally.” Last month, the Punjab government constituted a three-member high-powered committee to review the investigation into the murder, in which Hina’s husband and domestic servant have been sent on judicial remand . The committee has already visited Rawalpindi, questioned the deceased woman’s husband and domestic servant at Adiala Jail, met her family and inspected the crime scene. Separately, the National Assembly Standing Committee on Interior and Narcotics Control has summoned the Punjab inspector general of police and other senior police officials to brief it on the investigation. The committee meeting is scheduled for Thursday, Oct 29 at 2pm in the committee room at Parliament House, Islamabad.

items.title: War of words over Xinjiang erupts between Chinese and Turkish social media users

items.title: Do Miracles Really Happen?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Carlos Eire arrived in Miami at age 11 in 1962, a refugee from Castro’s Cuba. Three years passed before his mother could join him, and he never saw his father again. This experience of dislocation profoundly shaped Eire’s work as a religious historian. In his latest book, They Flew , Eire looks at early modern reports of miracles. Drawing on his own experience of moving between cultures and worldviews, he tries to imagine himself into the minds of those who claimed to have witnessed levitations, bilocations, and other impossible occurrences, and he asks what we can learn by taking these reports seriously. David Brooks talks with Eire about magic, empathy, and the past as a foreign country. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: This is a conversation about radical empathy. We live in a polarized age, often with people whose modes of consciousness are utterly alien to our own. We hear someone spew a conspiracy theory or utter an opinion that seems monstrous, and we think: How on earth can they think that way? But being a good citizen in this sort of pluralistic society requires that kind of radical empathy. It means approaching those who are different with a willingness and an ability to stand in their standpoint, to enter into, at least a little, how they see the world. My guest is Carlos Eire, who has been trained by life to excel at this. When he was a boy, he was airlifted out of Cuba by parents who wanted to get him away from Castro’s revolution. He worked his way through college, got a Ph.D. here at Yale, where he is now a professor of history and religious studies, and began a double-barreled career. On the one hand, he entered into the minds of people living in the late Middle Ages, describing how they thought about death and demons. But alongside his academic work, Carlos also wrote two popular memoirs about his childhood, Waiting for Snow in Havana , which won a National Book Award, and Learning to Die in Miami . We’re going to talk about his travels across worldviews. We’re going to spend the bulk of this time on Carlos’s recent book, They Flew . We’re going to look at the testimonies of 16th- and 17th-century religious figures who claimed they could levitate. When I started reading the book, these claims seemed totally bonkers to me. But take the time to get inside their heads. Learn to see the world through alien eyes. I think you’ll find Carlos generously curious and gently wise. You may not leave this podcast thinking that humans can float into the ceiling, but I bet you’ll learn a few things about how to enter other people’s minds. Carlos Eire, welcome to The Permanent Questions . Thanks so much for crossing New Haven to get here. Carlos Eire: Thanks very much. Thank you very much for inviting me. Brooks: Let me try to lay out what I was hoping to accomplish. I sort of see this as about empathy, about encountering people who are completely unlike yourself and trying to see the world from their point of view. This strikes me as a pretty necessary skill to have in a pluralistic society like ours. I think for most of the time, we’ll talk about this book, They Flew , which is a history of the impossible and possibly the most audacious book I’ve ever read. We’ll get to that, but let’s start with the leaving of Cuba. The simplest way to introduce your story is: Tell me about Operation Peter Pan. Eire: Yes, it received that unfortunate name. It didn’t have a name for us who went through it. Between New Year’s Day 1961 and mid-October 1962, slightly over 14,000 unaccompanied Cuban children came to the US. The plan was always to reunite with our parents either there, if the dictatorship ended, or here. It was well-organized chaos. There’s no other way to describe it. The 14,000 of us were sent to 48 different states eventually. Brooks: And you were 11. Eire: I was 11 when I left, and I left with my brother, who was 14. We went through a series of foster homes in Miami at first because we didn’t have family, not yet. And my first foster family—beautiful family, I consider them saints, Norma and Lou Chait—were Jewish, and I thought I had it made now because, at that age, I didn’t like going to church. But no, they forced me to go to church, and gave me money to put into the collection basket. I learned English really fast because they had zero Spanish. So I ended up learning English and a few Yiddish words that I thought were English. I later discovered, when I moved to Bloomington, Illinois, that people didn’t understand what I was saying. Long story with many ins and outs. My brother and I also ended up spending nine months in a home for juvenile delinquents because there was no other place for us. It was supposed to be temporary, but they kind of forgot about us. Brooks: The regime was sending kids to the Soviet Union. Eire: Yes. And it had happened before in Spain during the Civil War. There were so many Spanish immigrants in Cuba, including my grandparents, who had a vivid memory of kids who never returned. So panic set in. And also for any male over 18—military service. Of course, these parents, my own included, it wouldn’t have crossed their minds that this would go on forever, that the regime would not collapse. That was a big surprise to everyone. There’s no fixed statistic on how many children left whose parents were unable to leave. Mine were among them. My mom, it took her three and a half years to finally come to the US, and my father never made it out. I never harbored ill feelings of any sort. Ever since day one, I have thanked my parents for making that choice. I know there are a few who couldn’t understand. But for me, it’s always been a sacrifice they made. Brooks: There was a famous book written in the ’80s by a guy named David Lowenthal called The Past Is a Foreign Country. His argument is: We have to understand these people are different than us. But his second point was that it’s not only that the past is a foreign country, but that our relationship to the past has changed. We think of it as a line. It’s moving forward; it’s not moving back. But in previous eras, you go to any art museum, they’re dressing Jesus in 16th-century garb. They’re mingling the eras. Time is going backward and forward. They have a different attitude. So does that concept—the past is a foreign country—is that something that resonates with you, humbles you, different views of the past? Eire: Yes. I mean, having that experience of getting off the plane at the Miami airport back in 1962, you know, experiencing all this. Definitely another country—I’m in another country. The past is a lot like that. There are things that are difficult to understand about the past, especially cultural dimensions that no longer exist. What people could say, what people did and could do, and not only that—the worldview. The worldview above everything else, because that’s what I have focused on in all of my work as a historian is the cultural-religious dimension, the worldview that changed in the 16th century. I did have, however, I thought, an advantage over my American colleagues when it came to studying the Protestant Reformation, which was the revolution. I understood it as a revolution. And I saw many things happening in the early years of the Protestant Reformation that to me seemed only slightly different from the present. So it’s almost like I was a time traveler, right? And it was not a foreign country to me, for instance, to learn about the consistory in Calvin’s Geneva, which policed everyone’s behavior. I know what that’s like. And then when I went on to study the Spanish Inquisition, same thing. I’ve lived through this. People being ostracized for thinking incorrectly about some minor point—I’ve lived through that. That was not a foreign country to me. But when it comes to big items like belief in miracles, belief in witches, belief in demonic possession, all the supernatural stuff, of course it’s changed tremendously, but not entirely. The paradoxical challenge every historian faces is that something might look very similar to you, but it ends up not being all that similar. For instance, I spent a long time reading last wills and testaments from 16th-century Madrid. And I found one that I said, “Oh, they’re just like us.” This woman was bequeathing her little precious dog to so and so. But everyone was requesting hundreds of masses for their soul, sometimes thousands of masses. I even had a few last wills and testaments where the individual was listing as their only heir their soul. Brooks: Oh, really? Eire: Yes. And it sounds funny in English: The soul was the sole heir. But honestly, yes. Including one, I said, “This is a totally different world.” One priest who put it into his will. He says, “I know my family’s going to object, but they never did anything for me. I did this all on my own. This is my money.” And then I thought, “Well, now I’m back in this world.” So you get these mixed messages. It is very, very gratifying to find traces of human emotion like that lady willing her dog to her friend. It was a friend that she trusted. Brooks: I read that in the Middle Ages, and your period is sort of in the late Middle Ages, the emotions were more on the surface. I don’t know if this is measurable. But when they were in joy, they were in ecstasy. When they were in despair—the emotional register was much more vivacious than ours. Eire: It could be. Of course it depends on time and place and everything else that’s going on around people. But yes, I think that’s true. There was a lot of violence. A student of mine ended up doing his dissertation on violence in 16th-century Spain, looking at a very small town where all the records survived. People were fighting, like physically fighting, all the time. Then I understood why I had so many wills from people who were on their deathbed with head injuries. These emotions in the past, in one way, had to be dulled much more than with us. For instance, executions were public. And it wasn’t a nice execution. It was usually people being beheaded or hung or tortured. People lived through this. We would think immediately: Well, everyone there watching this is going to be severely traumatized . And perhaps they were, right? Brooks: They seem pretty happy in the accounts. Eire: People are cheering and clapping. Another world, another country. Absolutely. Brooks: This is one I’ve always wondered about. You’ve written about death, as you said. There’s an argument that you occasionally hear that so parents lost so many children that the loss of a child was not as emotionally crushing as it is for moderns. I sort of find that hard to believe. Eire: I do too. I think that’s somebody in the present saying, “It must have been that way. They had to.” But no, I don’t think so. We have plenty of evidence from diaries. There’s one diary that’s a tanner in Barcelona, 17th century, who lived through a plague in Barcelona. All his children died. And you can tell in the diary, it really hit him. Also, bringing it to the present, he actually wrote in his diary that the one child who survived was his least favorite. And why did it have to be that way? Brooks: There’s an argument that you raise in the book, though I don’t think you endorse it, that all these beliefs—whether in miracles, demonic possession, all that kind of stuff—it was functional for the period; it served some function. You quote a historian, Keith Thomas: “Belief in magic and miracles was an absolute necessity in premodern times due to ‘a preoccupation with the explanation and relief of human misfortune.’” Life was so hazardous that believing in all this stuff was part of the way they handled the hazardousness of their lives. Eire: And I think there’s truth in that, but I don’t think that’s all that’s going on. I was trained to be a functionalist. If there’s anything weird happening, anything supernatural happening, you just don’t go there. You bracket that. You don’t ask the question: Well, was this person really floating in the air or not? You analyze what function that belief served in that culture. But I have rebelled against my functionalist training. Brooks: Yeah, I’ll say big time. We get now to They Flew , and I started this book—it’s really a story of testimonies about levitation and bilocation, which is a person saying they were in two places at once. And I started this book with, I’m sure, the normal attitude you have encountered everywhere. One, people don’t levitate. It’s all a myth. And two, I’m not that interested. Why should I care about something that didn’t happen? Then I start reading the book, and I’m reading the testimonies and entering that other world. My mind is blown. If I were talking to somebody and reading testimonies like this in a current U.S. court of law, I would think they were pretty compelling. So describe to us what those testimonies were like and what the circumstances were. Eire: As a historian, I would’ve felt immensely uncomfortable arguing in any way that these things really happened if I didn’t have the right kind of testimonies. It’s all based on testimonies. Actually, for this time period that I work in, the early modern period, we have an advantage over the medieval period in that—especially in the Catholic world, the part of the world that remained Catholic—the process for identifying saints was made more rigorous in this time period. So the canonization process, which involves several sets of inquests, interviewing the people who knew this person, they include a section on miracles. But every answer that anyone gives in that inquest is sworn testimony, and the penalty’s not just a fine or some time behind bars. It’s hell, for lying. Most of the testimonies—not most, in some cases just many—come from very, very religious people, even clerics and nuns. So are these people going to perjure themselves, if they believe in hell? Brooks: These were not just unlettered people. Some of these testimonies are from the intellectual elite. And they’re saying, “Oh, so and so levitated.” Or they’re describing their own experiences, and there are tons of witnesses. I still don’t believe they levitated, but the testimony is … Eire: Well, we’re faced with a conundrum, which can be explained away in various ways. I’ve read one analysis of Joseph of Cupertino, this flying friar, the guy who spent more time in the air than anyone else in history: He was an acrobat. He had trained his muscles so well, like a gymnast, that he could make these great leaps. But no, he was suspended in the air, for heaven’s sake. And there are fakes. I have a whole section in the book about frauds, people who were caught faking all of this. Because as I said, it’s always been a case that people can fake these things. Magicians fake it all the time on stage. But faking it outdoors in the 16th or 17th century, that’s a little harder to do without ropes and pulleys or wires or anything. So we’re left with these testimonies, and what do we do with these testimonies? They are part of the past. Almost every time I’ve spoken about this book in public, the question comes up. I’ve had other historians bring it up, and other historians who share my point of view that we should take these testimonies very seriously. There is definitely a correlation throughout history, including the present—the correlation between the matrix of belief that a culture has and the frequency with which these anomalous phenomena occur. Brooks: What do you mean by that: “the matrix of belief”? What do you mean? Eire: If, let’s say, belief in levitation specifically is prevalent in a culture, you’re going to get more levitations. If belief in levitations is laughed at, as it is in our culture, you’re gonna have fewer. The same goes for any miraculous event. Brooks: I found the most compelling set of testimonies came from Teresa of Ávila. So could you tell us who she was and how she levitated? Eire: Teresa of Ávila, 16th century, was a Carmelite nun who from her 40s on had continuous ecstatic religious experiences, mystical ecstasies. Some of them involved levitation. She is one of the few levitators who has given us first-person accounts of what it feels like and what’s going on. So we have great detail on that from her end, from the personal end. Plus we have all these eyewitnesses, which were the nuns that she lived with and people who visited the convent, who testify to these incredible levitations. And she actually resisted these levitations. That’s another curious twist in her story. She begged God to stop it. She came right out and said to God, “Why are you doing this? What purpose does this serve?” And they stopped. She tells us in her autobiography they stopped. But that part of her autobiography she ended in 1562. The levitations came back again, with less frequency, but they came back again. She doesn’t write about it. She doesn’t complain about these. She’s complaining about the early ones. Brooks: I think her testimony is not like, “Look at me and what I did.” Her testimony is just like, “Here’s what it felt like.” I’m gonna read a few just so people get a sense: “At the highest point of rapture, one will neither see nor hear nor perceive. None of the soul’s faculties are able to perceive or know what is taking place.” So she’s describing that something goes blank. And then the resisting: “When I tried to resist these raptures, it seemed to me that I was being lifted up by a force beneath my feet so powerful that I know nothing to which I can compare it, for it came with much greater intensity than any other spiritual experience. I felt I was being torn to shreds, for it is a mighty struggle.” So these are physically demanding, arduous things. And then she’s bothered because she’s turning into a little celebrity for floating around the rooms, and this is the last thing she wants. And so she said, “There was no way of avoiding them, even in public. And then the persecutions and the murmurings follow. I have found some common threads linking all the levitators from this period who are eventually declared to be the genuine thing—that this is divine; this is not demonic. One of them is what Teresa describes, this cataleptic seizure, where you lose your senses, just vanish, and you don’t sense anything that’s going on around you, and then your body stiffens in whatever position. Sometimes these levitators go up, they’re praying on their knees, and they go up, and their knees are bent. And people actually try to unbend them, and they report that they can’t. I had a conversation here at the Yale Divinity School some months ago with a neurologist about all this stuff. It’s a very interesting conversation because he pointed to this spot on his head, and he says, “I can tell you exactly where these nuns are having these experiences.” And yes, you can pathologize as much as you want. If it were just a person telling you, “I felt this,” then it would be entirely explained. No more questions asked. But to have people say, “We saw this happen,” and to have it under oath, not just once but multiple times—then I think you need some other angle. You need to take this from another angle or another perspective and say that something is going on here that we, in our culture, none of us have been prepared to accept as a real possibility. Brooks: One of the beauties of the book is your first job as a historian is not to judge. It’s just to witness. Just look. What are they talking about? How are they thinking about this? And I have found that the biggest bias in media, maybe in the academy too, is not a left or right bias. It’s: What do people at dinner parties that people like me go to talk about? And if you have a category outside what people like me talk about, you are rejected. So as you’re writing this book, taking this stuff seriously, you must have been aware a lot of people are gonna think you’re crazy. Eire: Yes, but I’m used to that. And actually, back to the first part of our talk, I’m used to it because being in academia, for decades, if I could do it, I would hide the fact that I was Cuban from my colleagues. Because every time I said I was Cuban, I would get a little speech about how wonderful the revolution was. And if I said anything that was negative, all of a sudden, you’re not okay. You’re not okay. So I was used to that. Also, any person who has a religious life of any kind, the dominant culture, it does not accept your way of living as normal with a capital N . So you get used to that after a while. But having people dislike what I have to say is something that I’m used to. Brooks: You write at one point in They Flew : “Ask any historian why they write the kind of history they do, and if they are honest, they will tell you that when all is said and done, the history they write has everything to do with their life story, their yearnings, and their obsessions. This author is no different.” What does that mean? How do I interpret your decision to go into late medieval history? Eire: All my work as a historian has focused, in different ways, on the same subject, which is my obsession, which is, at bottom, the marrow of religion, as far as belief is concerned. There is some other dimension that is, for lack of a better term, more real than this, from which this dimension is derived. Brooks: And are you testing that proposition, or are you convinced by primordial faith that this proposition is true, and you’re trying to see how it works out? Eire: When I started out, and even now, I’ve had my ups and downs about that visceral kind of affirmation. That it’s not rational or purely intellectual. So that’s been constant, but it’s gone up and down. But the older I’ve become, the more that that has seemed very real to me. But the fact is, yes, belief is different from knowledge that you acquire through normal cognitive processes. Which is another reason that—I’ve also been obsessed looking at the phenomenon of mysticism. It’s the ecstasies that drew me to this subject first. It’s the claim, the existential claim people make to have experienced something other, with a capital O . Brooks: You can argue about whether people are flying up in the air, but there really are mystics. We all know people who have a mystical tongue or a mystical sense that I will never experience, but I know them and I see them, and I watch them. Eire: It’s the same with, let’s say, a musical virtuoso or an athletic virtuoso. That’s what at this advanced age of mine I’ve come to realize—that gifts are unevenly spread. Religion is one of these. There are people who just are spiritually gifted. And there are some who are spiritually blind and deaf, who just can’t even conceive of. I’ve often used this in my mysticism class, the believability of any mystic’s accounts of what it’s like to experience the divine. They all tell you the same thing, at least in the Christian tradition, but also in other religious traditions: “I can’t explain it to you.” It’s like explaining color to a blind person. How do you go about explaining color? No, it’s just another perception, another way of perceiving. What I still find fascinating is when those experiences which go beyond normal cognition have some physical impact on the person having it. Brooks: Yeah, I, I’ve seen friends who are—they’re moving, they’re kneeling. They’re not even thinking about it. They don’t know you were looking at them. They’re speaking sort of in tongues or some sort of other language. I don’t think it proves a belief in God, but it proves the existence of some sort of spiritual faculty that people have. I wanted to talk about the context in which Teresa’s living and a lot of the people in this 16th-, 17th-century period. This is a moment when science is beginning to take off, and you get Descartes, and I suppose go a little later you get Newton. This is reason and science taking off. Technology’s beginning to move up. It’s exactly this moment, as you make the point in the book, that these mystical experiences and these levitations begin to hit back. And it could be that there’s just intense pressure. They’ve hit a civilizational fork in the road, and they’re either gonna go off in the rationalist direction, or they’re gonna stay the way they were. And the crass way to put it, which I don’t want to reduce it just to this, is if you’re a Carmelite nun, you think, “Okay, you guys got calculus. That’s impressive, but we fly around the room.” Eire: I can’t argue against this way of looking at things. It makes sense, yes. I think it’s highly probable that you have this heightened sensibility toward the miraculous as a response not just to emerging science, but more immediately, at first, the Protestant Reformation, which is denying that all of these things are divine. But then along comes the scientific revolution. And yes, it is a natural response that people focus more intensely on these things. And as I said before, there seems to be this very common linkage between the matrix of belief and the frequency of these things happening. That’s a very solid, very rational argument, but it doesn’t explain everything. It just doesn’t. If in fact these things are happening and continued to happen, albeit with less frequency, you’re still dealing with a phenomenon. As I have discovered lately, there’s a word now being used to describe human beings who claim to have encountered nonhuman intelligence, and that word is experiencer . That’s also used for mystics. So in essence, a mystic telling you, “I understood the Trinity perfectly, but I can’t tell you” has the same trouble being believed as somebody who says, “This gray alien walked into my hotel room last night.” Brooks: There’s a famous episode which is sort of this clash. Rene Descartes, he’s early 17th century, he is actually a believer, but he decides he’s gonna sweep away all this tradition and knowledge that’s built up, and he’s gonna start from scratch. He’s gonna use pure reason, just logical, follow one step after another, and he makes sure he’s shielded from emotion. God forbid he should love somebody. And he’s trying to build up the whole edifice of human knowledge. And at exactly the same time, this other guy in France, Blaise Pascal, takes a look at what Descartes is doing and immediately hates him. Blaise Pascal is no random humanist. He was one of the greatest mathematicians to ever live. He was a technologist. He built a sort of early calculating machine. He was a scientist. He studied vacuums. So he had scientific rigor on his side, and he was saying, “I’m not against Descartes’s reason, but I have many other forms of knowledge that I use to understand the world.” The “spirit of genius” and the “spirit of finesse,” I think he called it. And he famously said, “The heart has reasons that reason knows not of.” And so he’s saying to Descartes, “You’re taking away other ways of knowing . ” And I think the clinching argument—it’s so amazing he understood this right away. We’re at this civilizational fork in the road. He says the problem with rationalism is not its admiration for reason, but its failure to recognize any other kind of knowledge. He’s saying, “You’re amputating me.” He’s talking out of his own experience of how he has studied the world. Eire: Plus he had a mystical experience. Brooks: Famously at the Night of Fire. Eire: Sewn into the lining of his coat: God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers. This distinction being made between these two forms of cognition. I’m so glad you brought up Pascal because he’s a contemporary. But there’s so many. When you’re dealing with the past—again, a different country—you find anomalous synchronicities all the time. One of the witnesses to St. Joseph of Cupertino’s levitations was a Saxon prince, Johann Friedrich of Saxony. And not just any Saxony, the Saxony that Luther had been part of. For some reason, he’s in Italy, and nobody has figured out what he was doing there. But he sees Joseph of Cupertino up in the air and he converts to Catholicism. Johann Friedrich. Oh my God. This is the same man who hired Leibniz as his librarian. Did he and Leibniz ever meet in the hallway, so to speak? And to talk about these things? A little thought experiment that I engage in my book: Yes, Newton and Joseph Cupertino walked the Earth, the same time. What if Newton had taken time off and done the grand tour and run into Joseph Cupertino? They could have. Yes, but they didn’t. They just didn’t. And Newton spent much of his later life trying to figure out the law of prophecy. Brooks: So we’re talking about this crucial time in Western history at least, where science is moving, and faith is moving in a different way. It seems to me you could look over periods of scientific advance—faith rises to respond. And so the period I know best is the late 19th century, the Industrial Revolution. You’ve got these machines. In the late 19th century, Henry Adams, who was in the same family as John Quincy Adams and John Adams, he goes to a bunch of world fairs. And he sees what they were obsessed with in the Chicago World’s Fair. And in the 13th century, the Virgin was a tremendous power source in Europe, and we get all these cathedrals that they were wanting to buy ’cause the Virgin was their power source. And he says, “That’s going away.” And he writes in that chapter—humans have a tendency to worship power sources, and people are gonna start worshiping machines. It’s not clear what he thinks about it, but at the exact same moment, there are a lot of other people, or roughly in that industrial period, who really mined it. And then the part I hadn’t clued in until reading your book, ’cause you mentioned this, at exactly this moment, late 19th century, a lot of the world goes gaga over seances. People you wouldn’t expect, like Arthur Conan Doyle, the founder of Sherlock Holmes, Mr. Rational. You mention Abraham Lincoln’s wife. A lot of serious people were sitting around doing seances and Ouija boards and stuff like that. Eire: And that’s kind of the tip of the iceberg because this is the same period that gives us the Latter-day Saints, the Millerites, and eventually the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Theosophy, which becomes immensely popular. Brooks: Explain what that is. Eire: Theosophy is a blend of Western occult mysticism with basically Hinduism and Buddhism. And it was enormously popular, here in the United States, but also throughout the world. The American Theosophical Society, which for a while was based in Philadelphia, sent missionaries all around the world. I learned this from a dissertation I read back when I was at the University of Virginia. Otherwise, I would not have found this fact, which I find fascinating: The two most successful missions that the American Theosophical Society had were Brazil and Cuba. But they’re also immensely popular throughout Europe. Anyway, the list could be longer of all these other things.
